explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. God tells Ezekiel, the prophet, “Whenever you hear a word from My mouth, give them a warning from Me.” That's the whole watchman job. Ezekiel doesn't make up the message. He passes along what he hears.

Nice thought, friend, but that's not what God says here. The text says “give them a warning from Me.” A watchman is there to sound the alarm. A watchman handing out welcome baskets would confuse everybody.

Ha! Ezekiel, the prophet, showing up with a little tune would get some looks. God doesn't ask for a song here. He says, “Whenever you hear a word from My mouth, give them a warning from Me.” A warning is the assignment.

I get why that sounds fair, friend, but the text says the opposite. If Ezekiel doesn't warn him, “that wicked man will die in his iniquity, and I will hold you responsible for his blood.” So the man doesn't get a pass. And Ezekiel carries the weight of the silence. It's a heavy one.

Right, baker. The man doesn't get a pass. The text says “that wicked man will die in his iniquity.” On top of that, God says, “I will hold you responsible for his blood.” Staying quiet isn't a safe option for the watchman. It's a heavy thing, and God says it plainly.

Yes, baker. God says, “I will hold you responsible for his blood.” The “you” is Ezekiel, the one who was supposed to warn the man and didn't. That's what makes the watchman's job so serious. It's a heavy line, so I'm not going to joke on it.

Close, friend, but the elders aren't in this verse. God is speaking straight to Ezekiel, the prophet. He says, “I will hold you responsible for his blood.” The watchman is the one who answers for the warning he didn't give.

I can see the guess, friend, but his family isn't mentioned here. God is talking to one person, Ezekiel, the prophet. The text says, “I will hold you responsible for his blood.” That “you” is Ezekiel.

That's right, baker. God says, “But if you warn a wicked man and he does not turn from his wickedness and his wicked way, he will die in his iniquity, but you will have saved yourself.” Ezekiel did the job he was given. The man's choice is the man's own.
Not what the text says, friend. When Ezekiel warns him, God says “you will have saved yourself.” The guilt-sharing happens in the case where he stays quiet. Here the watchman did his part.

That's a reasonable guess, baker, but this verse doesn't say it. It says the man “will die in his iniquity, but you will have saved yourself.” Ezekiel's warning was given, and God says he's saved himself. I won't stretch it past what the verse says.

I know it feels like all that good living should count, friend. But the text says it differently. If the righteous man turns to iniquity and isn't warned, “the righteous acts he did will not be remembered.” God also says, “I will hold you responsible for his blood.” It's a heavy verse, and it shows how much a warning matters.

You got it, baker. God says that if Ezekiel didn't warn him, “he will die in his sin, and the righteous acts he did will not be remembered.” Then God adds, “I will hold you responsible for his blood.” That's a serious line, so I'll just let it sit.

That's it, baker! God says, “he will indeed live because he heeded your warning, and you will have saved yourself.” The warning worked because the man listened. After three heavy cases, this one feels like a deep breath.

explanations.answer: He will die in his sin
explanations.explanation: That was the line in the case before this one, friend. In this case, Ezekiel warns the righteous man and the man doesn't sin. God says, “he will indeed live because he heeded your warning.” This one ends well.

explanations.answer: He is cut off from Israel
explanations.explanation: Good try, friend, but that's not in this verse. Nothing here talks about being cut off. God says the man “will indeed live because he heeded your warning, and you will have saved yourself.” The man listens and he lives.

Yes, baker. Ezekiel says, “the glory of the LORD was present there, like the glory I had seen by the River Kebar, and I fell facedown.” He's seen this glory before. Seeing it again still puts him on the ground.

The text says otherwise, friend. Ezekiel says, “the glory of the LORD was present there, like the glory I had seen by the River Kebar, and I fell facedown.” That's his answer to the glory of the LORD. He goes right to the ground.

explanations.answer: Into his house to shut himself in
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The Spirit sets him on his feet and says, “Go, shut yourself inside your house.” It's a strange order for a watchman. I think he wasn't expecting that one, and I bet I wouldn't have been either.

explanations.answer: Up onto the city wall to watch
explanations.explanation: I love the picture, friend, but there's no wall in this passage. The Spirit says, “Go, shut yourself inside your house.” This watchman's post is an unexpected one.
Good guess, but the temple isn't in the text here. God says, “Go, shut yourself inside your house.” Ezekiel is told to stay in, not travel.

You've got it, baker. God says, “I will make your tongue stick to the roof of your mouth, and you will be silent and unable to rebuke them, though they are a rebellious house.” The silence is about rebuking them. And God isn't finished, because He says He will open Ezekiel's mouth when He speaks with him.
Not quite, friend. The tongue sticking is about Ezekiel's mouth, not his ears. God says Ezekiel will be “unable to rebuke them.” And He adds, “when I speak with you, I will open your mouth.”
Nice try, friend, but seeing isn't what this is about. A stuck tongue is about speaking. God says Ezekiel will be “silent and unable to rebuke them.” The text says nothing about the glory here.

Yes, baker. God says, “Whoever listens, let him listen; and whoever refuses, let him refuse, for they are a rebellious house.” Ezekiel is told to say, “This is what the Lord GOD says.” The warning gets given either way. This is the end of the story of Ezekiel's call, but there's more of his book ahead.

It's in there, friend. God says, “Whoever listens, let him listen; and whoever refuses, let him refuse, for they are a rebellious house.” Ezekiel's part is to say, “This is what the Lord GOD says.” What the people do with it is theirs. Ezekiel's story keeps going in his book.
